title: Obligation, need, possibility and probability
subtitle: liable, compulsory, exempt, inevitable
summary: Learn the vocabulary of obligation (liable, mandatory, exempt), of need (necessity, shortage, requirements) and of possibility (opportunity, inevitable, doubtful).

lesson.heading: Obligation
lesson.text: Several rather formal words say that you have no choice. If you are **liable** for something, you are obliged to pay for it. If something is **mandatory** or **compulsory**, there is no alternative; if it is **optional**, you can choose.

examples.text: You will be **liable** for any damage when you rent a car.
The company is **obliged** to give a refund if the tour is cancelled.
The bank robbers **forced** him at gunpoint to open the safe.
We had **no choice/alternative but to** sell our house; we owed the bank a hundred thousand euros.

lesson.heading: Obligation words at a glance
rows: under an obligation to do something
made to do something against your will
no choice / no alternative but to
there is only one thing you can do
lesson.note: The death sentence is mandatory for drug-smuggling in some countries. Was sport compulsory at your school? No, it was optional. I am exempt from paying income tax as I'm a student.

lesson.heading: Need
lesson.text: The noun **need** takes the preposition **for**, not *of*. But the phrase **in need of** does use *of*. A **shortage** means there are not enough; **lack** means there is none or not enough.

examples.text: There's a **need for** more discussion on the matter.
This plant is **in need of** water.
examples.note: more formal than needs or wants

examples.text: She could not concentrate through **lack of** sleep.

lesson.heading: Necessity and requirements
lesson.text: A **necessity** is something you must have. If you can't manage without something, you **can't do without** it. **Requirements** are the things you must do or have in order to qualify for something.

examples.text: A car is an absolute **necessity** if you live in the countryside and there is no public transport.

examples.note: do without = survive or live without

examples.text: What are the **requirements** for a Master's course in English?

lesson.heading: Possibility and probability
rows: a real chance to do something
something that may happen (chance is less formal)

lesson.heading: Possibility in use
lesson.text: Notice the patterns: *It is doubtful **whether**...*, *It is probable **that**...*, and *an **opportunity to** do something*.

examples.text: I've been given an **opportunity** to work in Berlin.
Is there any **chance/possibility** you'll be free next week?
A rise in oil prices is **inevitable** as oil supplies run out.
It is **doubtful whether** the economy will improve next year.
Climate change is no longer just a possibility but is now an **absolute certainty**.

lesson.text: Compulsory and obligatory are near-synonyms; the opposite of both is optional, and if a rule does not apply to you at all, you are exempt from it.

exercises.prompt: Match the sentence beginnings with their endings.

pairs.left: People could not heat their homes

pairs.right: without a mobile phone these days.
for better day care for young children.

pairs.left: There is a list of requirements
pairs.right: for university entry on the website.

pairs.left: The whole house is in need

exercises.prompt: You don't have to buy the travel insurance; it's an ___ extra charge.
exercises.explanation: Optional means you can choose - the opposite of compulsory.

exercises.prompt: You can borrow the camcorder, but you will be ___ for any damage to it.
exercises.explanation: To be liable for something means to be obliged to pay for it.

exercises.prompt: No, he couldn't choose to pay a fine; a prison sentence is ___ for dangerous driving.
exercises.explanation: Mandatory means automatic, with no alternative.

exercises.prompt: I didn't want to do maths, but I had to. It's ___ in all secondary schools.
exercises.hint: (c... or o... = you must do it)
exercises.explanation: Compulsory and obligatory both mean that you must do something.

exercises.prompt: If you're unemployed, you're ___ from paying tax.
exercises.explanation: To be exempt from something means to be free from that obligation.

exercises.prompt: He didn't want to give them the money, but they had guns; they ___ him to hand it over.
exercises.explanation: Force someone to do something means to make them do it against their will.

exercises.prompt: We'll have to sell the house. I'm afraid we have ___; otherwise we will be bankrupt.
exercises.explanation: To have no choice / no alternative but to do something means there is only one option.

exercises.statement: If you are liable for something, it is your own responsibility.
exercises.explanation: Correct - to be liable for something means you are obliged to pay for it.

exercises.statement: 'There is a need of more qualified teachers' is correct English.
exercises.explanation: The noun need takes for: There is a need for more qualified teachers.

exercises.prompt: Most people consider that a mobile phone is not a luxury but an absolute ___.
exercises.explanation: A necessity is something you must have; you can't do without it.

exercises.prompt: I have been given an ___ to work with a team of zoologists in East Africa.
exercises.explanation: An opportunity is a real chance to do something.

exercises.prompt: Does the word say that something must happen, or only that it may happen?
